Not a scan target — reached transitively while fuzzing firecrawl/anydoc's xlsx cargo-fuzz target (seeded from anydoc's own test fixtures). Crash: 'attempt to multiply with overflow' at calamine-0.36.1/src/xlsx/mod.rs:2837, in get_row_and_optional_column (backs get_dimension/get_row_column/get_row — worksheet-dimension and merged-region parsing), reached via anydoc::formats::sheet::merged_regions parsing a crafted xl/worksheets/sheet1.xml. Root cause: the base-26 column and base-10 row accumulation loops used raw `*`/`+` with no length or bounds check, so an implausibly long letter/digit run (~20 chars) overflows u32 during accumulation and panics — before any bounds check gets a chance to run. A sibling parser in the same file (Reference::parse, used for cell-offset/range operations) already guards the identical input class correctly via wrapping_mul/wrapping_add + a post-hoc validate() against MAX_COLUMNS/MAX_ROWS; this function just never got the same protection, and its own callers don't do a follow-up bounds check the way Reference's constructors do. No PVR/SECURITY.md on the repo, but this is DoS-only (Rust panics safely, no memory corruption) with an obvious, minimal, convention-matching fix, so — per the same public-channel logic as an already-disclosed dependency CVE — fixed it directly rather than just filing a report: forked, patched both accumulation loops to checked_mul/checked_add returning the existing ColumnNumberOverflow/RowNumberOverflow errors (already defined and used by the sibling parser, no new error variant needed), added a regression test reproducing the exact crash plus the get_dimension call-path case, verified `cargo test --lib` (43 passed) and `cargo clippy --lib -- -D warnings` clean, opened tafia/calamine#705. The other 7 seeded anydoc fuzz targets (rtf, ppt, csv, docx, odf, epub, pdf; ~90s each) stayed clean throughout, 0 crashes — xlsx was the only one that turned up anything. Verified the fix locally end-to-end: patched anydoc's fuzz/Cargo.toml with a [patch.crates-io] path override to the fixed calamine fork (the override has to go in fuzz/Cargo.toml specifically — cargo-fuzz's fuzz/ directory has its own separate Cargo.lock, so a patch on the parent anydoc/Cargo.toml silently has no effect), ran `cargo update -p calamine` to pick it up, rebuilt, and re-ran the exact saved crash artifact: clean exit, no panic. UPDATE (2026-08-08, later same day): maintainer (jmcnamara) flagged this as likely the same bug as an already-open PR, #696 (krickert, opened 2026-07-27 — two weeks before this one, and already reworked once per maintainer feedback to validate against actual row/column limits rather than just catching the raw overflow). Confirmed same root cause, closed #705 as a duplicate rather than making the maintainer arbitrate between two competing fixes. The lesson worth carrying forward: check a target repo's own open PRs/issues for the exact bug class BEFORE filing, not just its advisory history — this would have caught #696 immediately (same function name, same file, same error variants) had it been checked. The anydoc-side dependency is still real and still needs fixing; it just lands via #696 once merged, not #705.

REAL FINDING, submitted via gh api POST security-advisories/reports: GHSA-m72w-8m4w-w85f, state triage. src/core/mcp_server.zig's HTTP handler auth check (~line 460) compares the client-supplied Bearer token against the configured token via std.mem.eql - Zig's standard, NON-constant-time comparison that short-circuits on the first mismatched byte, a genuine timing side-channel. Confirmed this is not just theoretical for this specific case: (1) server binds 0.0.0.0:9094/9095 by default per the README - all network interfaces, not localhost-only, (2) grepped the entire file for sleep/delay/rateLimit/attempts/lockout - found zero rate limiting or lockout anywhere in the auth path, no mitigating factor at all, (3) what the token protects is unusually high-value - successful token recovery grants full remote debugger control per the tool's own 84-tool feature list. Reported honestly with practical-severity caveats rather than oversold: network timing attacks are inherently noisy, need many samples per byte for a reliable signal, so this is a real vulnerability class with genuine but not instant exploitability, most practical against a target on a low-latency/local network (a plausible deployment scenario for reverse-engineering tooling). Suggested fix: constant-time comparison (XOR-accumulate over full length, or std.crypto.utils.timingSafeEql) for the token check specifically; separately suggested (not filed as a distinct vuln) binding 127.0.0.1 by default with 0.0.0.0 as explicit opt-in, to reduce exposure for the common single-machine use case. UPDATE 2026-08-24: maintainer closed as Not Applicable, and did real empirical work to back it rather than dismiss it - built an actual blind timing-attack PoC attempting byte-by-byte token recovery via response-time measurement, found the real per-byte timing signal from std.mem.eql is nanosecond-scale while genuine network/OS-scheduling jitter is 100-1000x larger (hundreds of microseconds), completely drowning the signal; PoC consistently recovered wrong token values across multiple runs. This is a legitimate, technically sound rebuttal, not a brush-off. LESSON: I correctly identified a real non-constant-time-comparison code pattern and correctly hedged in the report that timing attacks are noisy/non-trivial, but still filed it as a full severity finding based on the vulnerability CLASS being real rather than actually quantifying practical exploitability against this specific token length before submitting - should have either built/attempted a similar PoC myself first, or framed this explicitly as a minor hardening suggestion (constant-time comparison is still good practice regardless) rather than a severity-rated vulnerability report. The code pattern itself (std.mem.eql for a secret comparison) is still worth fixing as defense-in-depth, but calling it exploitable was the overclaim - don't cite this as a confirmed vuln in any future summary, cite it as 'raised and the maintainer demonstrated it's not practically exploitable, good example of an honest correction on this campaign.'
